title: Metadata Management
html:
1Definition and Goals

Definition: Planning, implementation, and control activities to enable access to high quality, integrated Metadata.

4 Goals:

  1. Provide organizational understanding of business terms and usage
  2. Collect and integrate Metadata from diverse sources
  3. Provide a standard way to access Metadata
  4. Ensure Metadata quality and security

Core Principle: One person's Metadata is another person's data (based on level of abstraction).

2Business Drivers

Reliable, well-managed Metadata helps:

  • Increase confidence in data by providing context and enabling measurement of data quality
  • Increase value of strategic information (e.g., Master Data) by enabling multiple uses
  • Improve operational efficiency by identifying redundant data and processes
  • Prevent use of out-of-date or incorrect data
  • Reduce data-oriented research time
  • Improve communication between data consumers and IT professionals
  • Create accurate impact analysis, reducing risk of project failure
  • Improve time-to-market by reducing SDLC time
  • Reduce training costs and lower impact of staff turnover through thorough documentation
  • Support regulatory compliance

Impact of Poorly Managed Metadata:

  • Redundant data and data management processes
  • Replicated and redundant dictionaries, repositories, and Metadata storage
  • Inconsistent definitions of data elements and risks of data misuse
  • Competing and conflicting sources/versions reducing confidence of data consumers
  • Doubt about the reliability of Metadata and data

3Eight Guiding Principles

  1. Organizational Commitment — Secure senior management support and funding as part of enterprise data asset strategy
  2. Strategy — Develop a Metadata strategy accounting for how Metadata will be created, maintained, integrated, and accessed; define requirements BEFORE evaluating/purchasing tools
  3. Enterprise Perspective — Take enterprise view for extensibility; implement through iterative and incremental delivery
  4. Socialization — Communicate necessity and purpose of each type of Metadata; socialization encourages business use and contribution of business expertise
  5. Access — Ensure staff know how to access and use Metadata
  6. Quality — Recognize Metadata is often produced through existing processes; hold process owners accountable for Metadata quality
  7. Audit — Set, enforce, and audit standards for Metadata to simplify integration and enable use
  8. Improvement — Create feedback mechanism so consumers can inform the Metadata Management team of incorrect or out-of-date Metadata

4Three Types of Metadata

Business Metadata

Focuses largely on the content and condition of the data, including data governance details.

  • Non-technical names and definitions of concepts, subject areas, entities, and attributes
  • Business rules, transformation rules, calculations, derivations
  • Data models, data quality rules and measurement results
  • Data provenance and data lineage; data standards
  • Valid value constraints; stakeholder contact information
  • Security/privacy levels; known data issues; usage notes

Technical Metadata

Provides information about the technical details of data, systems that store data, and processes that move it.

  • Physical database table and column names, column properties, database object properties
  • Access permissions; data CRUD rules; physical data models
  • ETL job details; file format schema definitions
  • Source-to-target mapping documentation; data lineage documentation
  • Content update cycle schedules and dependencies; recovery and backup rules

Operational Metadata

Describes details of processing and accessing data.

  • Logs of job execution for batch programs; history of extracts and results
  • Results of audit, balance, control measurements; error logs
  • Reports and query access patterns, frequency, and execution time
  • Backup, retention, date created, disaster recovery provisions
  • SLA requirements; volumetric and usage patterns; data archiving and retention rules; purge criteria

Alternative Library/Information Science Categories

Type Description
Descriptive Title, author, subject — enables identification and retrieval
Structural Relationships within/among resources (e.g., number of pages, chapters)
Administrative Version numbers, archive dates — manages resources over lifecycle

5ISO/IEC 11179 Metadata Registry Standard

  • Purpose: Framework for defining a Metadata registry to enable Metadata-driven data exchange, based on exact definitions of data elements
  • Key Parts:
    • Part 1: Framework for the Generation and Standardization of Data Elements
    • Part 3: Basic Attributes of Data Elements
    • Part 4: Rules and Guidelines for Formulation of Data Definitions
    • Part 5: Naming and Identification Principles for Data Elements
    • Part 6: Registration of Data Elements

6Sources of Metadata (15 Sources)

Source Key Fact
Business Glossary Documents business concepts, terminology, definitions, and relationships; 3 core audiences: Business Users, Data Stewards, Technical Users
Application Metadata Repositories Often built into modeling tools, BI tools, and other applications
BI Tools Produce Metadata: overview information, classes, objects, derived items, reports, distribution channels
Configuration Management Tools (CMDB) Manage IT assets, relationships, contractual details; each asset = Configuration Item (CI)
Data Dictionaries Define structure and contents of data sets; manage names, descriptions, structure, characteristics, relationships
Data Integration Tools Document lineage as data moves between systems; provide API for external Metadata repositories
Database Management / System Catalogs Describe DB content, sizing, software versions, deployment status, network/infrastructure availability
Data Mapping Management Tools Transform requirements into mapping specifications; used during analysis and design phase
Data Quality Tools Assess data quality through validation rules; exchange quality scores and profiles with Metadata repositories
Directories and Catalogs Contain information about systems, sources, and locations of data; useful to developers and data super users
Event Messaging Tools Move data between diverse systems; generate Metadata describing data movement
Modeling Tools and Repositories Build conceptual, logical, physical models; produce Metadata on subject areas, entities, attributes, relationships
Reference Data Repositories Document business values and descriptions of enumerated data types (domains)
Service Registries Manage technical information about services and service end-points (SOA); most important Metadata: service version, location, availability, deployment date
Other Metadata Stores Event registries, source lists, code sets, lexicons, spatial/temporal schema

Business Glossary — 3 Core Audiences

  1. Business Users (analysts, management, executives) — understand terminology and data
  2. Data Stewards — manage lifecycle of terms; associate data assets with glossary terms; resolve differences
  3. Technical Users — make architecture, design, and development decisions; conduct impact analysis

7Metadata Architecture Types (4 Types)

Centralized Architecture

  • Single Metadata repository containing copies of Metadata from various sources
  • Advantage: High availability, quick retrieval, Metadata can be transformed/enhanced
  • Limitation: Complex processes to replicate source changes; maintenance costly; custom extraction modules needed
  • Best for: Organizations with limited IT resources, seeking maximum automation

Distributed Architecture

  • No persistent repository; Metadata retrieval engine responds to requests in real time from source systems
  • Advantage: Metadata always as current as possible; no batch replication
  • Limitation: No user-defined Metadata entries; query capability depends on source system availability; no global search
  • Uses common object request broker or similar middleware

Hybrid Architecture

  • Combines centralized and distributed approaches
  • Metadata moves from source systems into centralized repository
  • Benefits: Near-real-time retrieval + enhanced Metadata; lowers manual IT intervention; global search available
  • Limitation: Source system availability still a limitation; additional overhead to link results with augmented Metadata
  • Best for: Organizations with rapidly-changing operational Metadata; those needing consistent, uniform Metadata

Bi-Directional Architecture

  • Advanced approach: Metadata can change in any part of the architecture (source, integration, UI)
  • Feedback coordinated from repository (broker) back into original source
  • Challenge: Must manage changes to source AND repository; additional process interfaces must be built and maintained

The three main approaches (centralized, distributed, hybrid) mimic approaches to designing data warehouses.

8Activities

Activity 1: Define Metadata Strategy

  • Describes how organization intends to manage Metadata and move from current to future state
  • 5 Steps:
    1. Initiate Metadata strategy planning — draft charter, scope, objectives; establish communications plan
    2. Conduct key stakeholder interviews
    3. Assess existing Metadata sources and information architecture
    4. Develop future Metadata architecture — target architecture for managed Metadata environment
    5. Develop phased implementation plan — document strategy; define phased approach

Activity 2: Understand Metadata Requirements

  • Content requirements: what Metadata is needed and at what level
  • 10 Functionality-focused Requirements:
    1. Volatility — how frequently attributes will be updated
    2. Synchronization — timing of updates relative to source changes
    3. History — whether historical versions need to be retained
    4. Access rights — who can access Metadata and how
    5. Structure — how Metadata will be modeled for storage
    6. Integration — degree of integration from different sources
    7. Maintenance — processes and rules for updating Metadata
    8. Management — roles and responsibilities
    9. Quality — Metadata quality requirements
    10. Security — some Metadata cannot be exposed (reveals existence of protected data)

Activity 3: Define Metadata Architecture

  • Key Principle: Managed Metadata environment should isolate end user from disparate sources; provide single access point
  • Users should access Metadata without awareness of differing environments

Create MetaModel:

  • Data model for Metadata repository (metamodel)
  • One of first design steps after strategy is complete
  • Two levels: high-level conceptual model (system relationships) and lower-level metamodel (attribute details)

Apply Metadata Standards:

  • Internal standards: naming conventions, custom attributions, security, visibility
  • External standards: data exchange formats, API design

Activity 4: Create and Maintain Metadata

  • Like other data, Metadata can be profiled and inspected for quality
  • Integration (Scanning) — Two Approaches:
    1. Proprietary interface: Single-step scan and load; collector calls format-specific loader directly
    2. Semi-proprietary interface: Two-step; scanner outputs format-specific data file; more open architecture

Delivery Mechanisms:

  • Metadata intranet websites for browse/search/query/reporting
  • Reports, glossaries, and documents
  • Data warehouses, data marts, and BI tools
  • Web services and APIs

Activity 5: Query, Report, and Analyze Metadata

  • Guide use of data assets; used in BI, business decisions, and business semantics
  • Report types include: change impact analysis, data lineage reports, troubleshoot varying definitions

9Techniques

Data Lineage and Impact Analysis

  • Two Lineage Types:

    • "As Implemented" Lineage — current version based on programming code
    • "As Designed" Lineage — lineage described in mapping specification documents

  • Stitching: Process of connecting lineage pieces from different tools; results in holistic visualization from original source to final destination

  • Two Discovery Strategies:

    1. Business Focus — start from target locations; trace back to sources; limited to prioritized data elements; pairs well with DQ measurements
    2. Technical Focus — start at source systems; identify all consumers downstream; enables impact reports ("What systems are impacted if column width changes?"); more complex to manage

Metadata for Big Data Ingest

  • Metadata tags applied to data upon ingestion into data lake
  • Data profiling during ingestion can identify: data domains, relationships, data quality issues
  • Tags can identify sensitive/private data (e.g., PII — Personally Identifiable Information)

10Tools

Metadata Repository Management Tools — Primary tool category:

  • Include integration layer and interface for manual updates
  • Metadata can be manually entered OR extracted through specialized connectors
  • Allow exchange of collected Metadata with other repositories
  • Enable enrichment and standardization of diverse Metadata as it moves between repositories

11Governance and Metrics

Process Controls

  • Governance team: defines standards, manages status changes, responsible for promotional activities and training
  • Maturity Progression Example: Candidate term → Approved → Published → Replaced/Retired

8 Suggested Metrics on Metadata Environments

Metric Description
Metadata Repository Completeness Compare ideal coverage (all artifacts and instances in scope) to actual coverage
Metadata Management Maturity Based on CMM-DMM (Capability Maturity Model) approach
Steward Representation Organizational commitment measured by appointment and coverage of stewards across enterprise
Metadata Usage Repository login counts; anecdotal/survey measures on qualitative usage
Business Glossary Activity Usage, update frequency, definition resolution, coverage
Master Data Service Data Compliance Shows reuse of data in SOA solutions
Metadata Documentation Quality Automatic methods: collision logic, percentage of attributes with definitions; Manual: random/complete survey
Metadata Repository Availability Uptime, processing time (batch and query)

Metadata Documentation — Master Catalog Should Include:

  • Metadata implementation status
  • Source and target Metadata store
  • Schedule information for updates
  • Retention and versions kept
  • Quality statements or warnings
  • System of record and other data source statuses
  • Tools, architectures, and people involved
  • Sensitive information and masking strategy

12Practice Q&A

Q1: What is the definition of Metadata Management? A: Planning, implementation, and control activities to enable access to high quality, integrated Metadata.

Q2: What are the 3 main types of Metadata? A: Business Metadata (content/condition), Technical Metadata (technical details of data and systems), Operational Metadata (processing and accessing details).

Q3: What are the alternative library/information science categories of Metadata? A: Descriptive (enables identification/retrieval), Structural (relationships within/among resources), Administrative (manages resources over lifecycle).

Q4: What are the 4 Metadata architecture types? A: Centralized (single repository), Distributed (real-time retrieval, no persistent repository), Hybrid (combined), Bi-Directional (advanced: changes in any part feed back to source).

Q5: What is a metamodel? A: The data model for a Metadata repository — one of the first design steps after strategy is complete.

Q6: What is the difference between "As Implemented" and "As Designed" lineage? A: "As Implemented" = current lineage based on programming code. "As Designed" = lineage described in mapping specification documents.

Q7: What is "stitching" in the context of Metadata? A: The process of connecting lineage pieces from different tools to create a holistic visualization from original source to final destination.

Q8: What is ISO/IEC 11179 and which part covers naming standards? A: Metadata Registry Standard providing a framework for Metadata-driven data exchange. Part 5 covers Naming and Identification Principles for Data Elements.

Q9: What are the 3 core audiences of a Business Glossary? A: Business Users (understand terminology), Data Stewards (manage lifecycle, resolve differences), Technical Users (architecture/design decisions, impact analysis).

Q10: What are the 8 guiding principles of Metadata Management? A: Organizational Commitment, Strategy, Enterprise Perspective, Socialization, Access, Quality, Audit, Improvement.

Q11: Which Metadata architecture type has NO persistent repository? A: Distributed Architecture — Metadata retrieved in real time from source systems.

Q12: What are the 4 goals of Metadata Management? A: Provide organizational understanding of business terms; collect and integrate Metadata from diverse sources; provide standard access to Metadata; ensure Metadata quality and security.

Q13: What is the Metadata Management maturity metric based on? A: CMM-DMM (Capability Maturity Model for Data Management).

Q14: What is the key principle for Metadata architecture design? A: Managed Metadata environment should isolate end users from disparate sources; provide a single access point where users can access Metadata without awareness of differing environments.

Q15: What are the two Metadata scanning/integration approaches? A: Proprietary interface (single-step scan and load) and Semi-proprietary interface (two-step: scan outputs a file, then load from that file; more open architecture).
